source_text:
In Ruth
ΡΟΥΘ.
12.989 Καὶ ὄνομα τῇ δευτέρᾳ Ῥούθ. Ῥοὺθ τύπον φέρει τῶν ἐθνῶν· ἥτις κατέλιπε τὰ
πάτρια, καὶ ἡνώθη τῇ Ἰσραηλιτικῇ ἕξει. Ζητητέον δὲ πῶς, τοῦ νόμου ἀπαγορεύοντος
μὴ εἰσελθεῖν Μοαβίτην εἰς Ἐκκλησίαν Θεοῦ, ἡ Ῥοὺς Μοαβίτις οὖσα εἰσῆλθε. Καὶ
τοῦτο ζητῶν χρῆσαι τῷ· "∆ικαίω δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ
ἀνυποτάκτοις."
thought_title: Ruth as a type of the Gentiles and the legal problem of her entry
orientation: Origen is opening his comment on Ruth 1:4, where the second daughter-in-law is named, and he raises the legal difficulty that the law forbids a Moabite from entering the assembly of God.
pass_a_gloss: And the name of the second was Ruth. Ruth bears a type of the Gentiles; she left behind the ancestral ways, and was joined to the Israelite way of life. But it must be inquired how, when the law forbids a Moabite not to enter into the assembly of God, Ruth, being a Moabite, entered. And inquiring into this, apply the saying: "But the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient."

choices.why: The glossary requires 'type' for τύπον, and φέρει is literal 'bears' rather than 'is a type' to preserve the verb's force.
ἕξις means a settled state or habit; 'habit' is literal and avoids the interpretive 'way of life' which is not in the source.
rejected: to the Israelite way of life

choices.why: The verbal adjective is impersonal and expresses necessity; 'it must be inquired' keeps the impersonal force.
χρῆσαι is a middle imperative meaning 'use/apply'; the dative τῷ points to the following quotation, so 'use the saying' makes the application explicit.
κεῖται is the standard legal term for a law being established or laid down; 'is not laid down' preserves the legal register.

bible_refs.note: ∆ικαίω δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ ἀνυποτάκτοις

pass_b_english: The second was named Ruth. Ruth bears a type of the Gentiles, because she left her ancestral ways behind and was joined to the Israelite way of life. But it must be inquired how Ruth, who was a Moabite, entered the assembly of God when the law forbids a Moabite to enter the assembly of God. And in inquiring into this, apply the saying: "The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient" (1 Timothy 1:9).

problems.quote: when the law forbids a Moabite to enter
problems.source_quote: τοῦ νόμου ἀπαγορεύοντος μὴ εἰσελθεῖν Μοαβίτην εἰς Ἐκκλησίαν Θεοῦ
problems.why: Missing 'assembly of God' after 'enter'; the destination is omitted.
problems.fix: when the law forbids a Moabite to enter the assembly of God
problems.ruling: English omits 'εἰς Ἐκκλησίαν Θεοῦ' ('assembly of God'); destination lost, misleading reader.

edits.old: when the law forbids a Moabite to enter.
edits.new: when the law forbids a Moabite to enter the assembly of God.

problems.why: Same Greek concept rendered two ways; reader may think different ideas.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'way of life' or 'manner of life'.

problems.why: Same verb rendered differently; minor but unnecessary variation.
Critical biblical quotation varies; 'lawless' vs 'unjust' are different concepts.
problems.fix: Check Greek and standardize; note variant if intentional.

problems.why: Same concept rendered differently across parallel versions; reader may think distinct ideas are meant.
problems.fix: Use one rendering consistently across all parallel sections.

problems.why: 'Habit' vs 'way of life' may suggest different concepts to a first-time reader.
Same Greek word rendered two ways; reader may miss that identical text is quoted.
Minor verb variation across parallel versions; not confusing but inconsistent.
problems.fix: Pick one verb and use it throughout.

The glossary issue about 'ancestral ways' is addressed by standardizing to 'ancestral ways'.

problems.fix: Standardize to one translation or note the variant.

problems.fix: Standardize or flag as synonymous variants.

problems.why: Shift from second-person imperative to participial construction changes voice.

problems.why: 1 Timothy 1:9 reads 'lawless and disobedient' or 'ungodly and sinners' in standard texts; 'unjust' is non-standard.
problems.fix: Verify Greek or standardize to accepted translation.

problems.why: Same concept rendered differently across parallel fragments; reader may think two distinct ideas are meant.
problems.fix: Use one rendering consistently across all parallel fragments.

problems.why: Same Greek word rendered 'lawless' vs 'unjust' across parallel fragments of the same 1 Tim 1:9 citation.
problems.fix: Use one rendering consistently; 'lawless' matches the standard translation of 1 Tim 1:9.

problems.fix: Standardize the phrasing across all parallel fragments.

last_rejected.quote: because she left her ancestral customs behind
last_rejected.why: 'ἥτις' is a generic relative ('who'), not causal ('because'); this changes the syntax from description to explanation.
last_rejected.fix: who left her ancestral customs behind
last_rejected.ruling: ἥτις can introduce causal/explanatory clauses; rendering as 'because' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: 'ἕξις' here means 'way of life/condition/character,' not 'habit' in the modern sense of a repeated practice; 'habit' is misleading.
last_rejected.ruling: ἕξις can mean 'habit/condition/way of life'; 'habit' is within the word's normal semantic range.

last_rejected.quote: But it must be inquired how Ruth
last_rejected.why: 'Ζητητέον' is impersonal ('it must be inquired'), but the English shifts to 'Ruth' as subject, making her the one who must inquire rather than the topic of inquiry.
last_rejected.fix: But it must be inquired how Ruth, a Moabite, entered
last_rejected.ruling: 'It must be inquired how Ruth...entered' is correct; Ruth is topic of inquiry, not inquirer. No error.

last_rejected.why: The Greek is a genitive absolute ('the law forbidding'), not a temporal clause ('when'); this changes the grammatical relationship.
last_rejected.fix: the law forbidding a Moabite to enter the assembly of God
last_rejected.ruling: Genitive absolute τοῦ νόμου ἀπαγορεύοντος rendered as 'when the law forbids' is standard and accurate.

last_rejected.quote: And as you inquire into this, use the saying
last_rejected.why: The Greek has no 'you'; 'ζητῶν' is a participle ('inquiring/seeking'), and 'χρῆσαι' is an imperative addressed to the reader/hearer. The English adds 'you' and makes it a suggestion rather than a command.
last_rejected.fix: And inquiring into this, apply: 'The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient'
last_rejected.ruling: χρῆσαι is imperative; 'use' conveys command. Adding 'you' is normal English for imperatives.

last_rejected.why: 'ἀδίκοις' means 'unjust/unrighteous,' not 'lawless'; 'lawless' is a mistranslation that conflates it with 'without law' (ἄνομος).
last_rejected.ruling: ἀδίκοις can mean 'unrighteous/lawless'; 'lawless' matches 1 Tim 1:9 KJV tradition. Within range.
